- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next period.
- If model shows sharp upward spike (e.g., >+5% from prior) and sentiment is weak or neutral, cap forecast at 1–2% below prior peak to avoid overshoot.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 70–72) after a spike, model often fails to correct; adjust forecast downward by 0.5–1.5% per day until trend stabilizes.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and model forecasts are rising, reduce forecast by 1–3% to reflect bearish sentiment.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overfits recent volatility; if last 3–5 days show high volatility, smooth forecast by averaging last 5–7 days’ values.
- If sentiment history shows rising optimism (e.g., 0.7–0.9) but model forecasts are flat or falling, model underestimates upside; add 0.5–1.5% to forecast to align with sentiment.
- If model consistently forecasts 1–2% above true outcome in early periods (e.g., first 5–7 days), apply a 1–2% downward bias to first 3–5 days of forecast.
